leads.text: JWE decompression bomb (zip bomb): jose/jwe.py:453 calls zlib.decompress(compressed) with NO max_length argument and no post-decompression size check. The attacker fully controls both the trigger and the payload via the JWE token passed to the jwe.decrypt() entry point: _jwe_compact_deserialize(jwe_str) (jwe.py:79) parses the raw token, header is json.loads()'d from the base64url header segment (jwe.py:276->300), and decrypt() then calls _decompress(header.get("zip"), plain_text) at jwe.py:187. The only guards in _decompress are name checks on the zip algorithm -- 'zip not in ZIPS.SUPPORTED' (line 448), 'zip is None' (450), 'zip == ZIPS.DEF' (452) -- none of which bound the output size. An attacker sets the protected header to {"alg":"RSA-OAEP","enc":"A256GCM","zip":"DEF"} and supplies a few KB of highly-compressible deflate data that expands to multiple GB, exhausting memory/CPU in the decrypting process. Because RSA-OAEP / RSA1_5 / ECDH-ES are PUBLIC-key encryption, any unauthenticated party holding the recipient's public key can mint a valid token, so this needs no shared secret. Fix: pass a bounded max_length to zlib.decompress (or use a decompressobj with an output cap) and reject oversized output.

leads.text: AES-CBC-HMAC padding oracle -- ciphertext is decrypted and PKCS7-unpadded BEFORE the MAC is verified. In jose/jwe.py:_decrypt_and_auth (method at line 208), line 239 runs 'plaintext = encryption_key.decrypt(cipher_text, iv, aad, auth_tag)' and only AFTERWARDS does line 240 check 'auth_tag != auth_tag_check' -> raise JWEError("Invalid JWE Auth Tag") (line 241). For the A*CBC-HS* encs (selected by 'enc in ALGORITHMS.HMAC_AUTH_TAG', line 230), the backend performs NO authentication at all: jose/backends/cryptography_backend.py CryptographyAESKey.decrypt (method line 490) takes the non-GCM branch at line 505 and runs Cipher(algorithms.AES(...), mode).decryptor() -> decryptor.update(cipher_text) (507) -> decryptor.finalize() (508) -> PKCS7(...).unpadder() (509) -> unpadder.update(padded_plain_text) (510) -> unpadder.finalize() (511). unpadder.finalize() raises on invalid PKCS7 padding, producing an error distinguishable from the later 'Invalid JWE Auth Tag' -- a classic padding oracle. cipher_text, iv and auth_tag are all attacker-controlled, split straight out of the token at jwe.py:273 and base64url-decoded. An attacker who can submit chosen JWE tokens and observe which error/latency results can decrypt ciphertext byte-by-byte without the key. Fix: verify the HMAC over (aad||iv||ciphertext||al) in constant time and abort BEFORE invoking any CBC decryption or unpadding (encrypt-then-MAC ordering, per RFC 7518 5.2.2.2).

leads.text: Non-constant-time comparison of the JWE authentication tag: jose/jwe.py:240 (in _decrypt_and_auth, method line 208) compares the attacker-supplied tag against the computed HMAC with a plain Python inequality -- 'auth_tag != auth_tag_check' -- rather than hmac.compare_digest. Python's bytes __eq__ short-circuits on the first differing byte, leaking via timing how many leading bytes of the attacker's guess match the real HMAC, which lets an attacker forge a valid tag byte-by-byte over many requests. auth_tag is attacker-controlled (split from the token at jwe.py:273, base64url-decoded) and auth_tag_check is the secret-derived HMAC from _auth_tag(cipher_text, iv, aad, mac_key, key_len) at jwe.py:232. This is grounded as an inconsistency, not a guess: a graph-wide search shows this codebase uses the constant-time primitive in exactly ONE place -- jose/backends/native.py:69 'hmac.compare_digest(sig, self.sign(msg))' for JWS HMAC verification -- and nowhere in the JWE path. Fix: use hmac.compare_digest at jwe.py:240.

leads.text: Attacker-controlled UNVERIFIED 'alg' header selects the at_hash digest algorithm and can raise an unhandled KeyError. jose/jwt.py:146 reads the algorithm straight out of the unauthenticated token header -- 'algorithm = jws.get_unverified_header(token)["alg"]' -- and passes it to _validate_claims(..., algorithm=algorithm, ...) at jwt.py:156, where it is used as a raw dict index at jwt.py:448: 'calculate_at_hash(access_token, ALGORITHMS.HASHES[algorithm])'. Two consequences: (1) the hash used to validate the at_hash binding between the ID token and the access token is chosen by the attacker, so an attacker able to influence the at_hash claim can steer validation toward the weakest available digest instead of the one the issuer actually used; (2) if 'alg' names a supported signing algorithm that has no entry in ALGORITHMS.HASHES, the subscript raises KeyError, which is NOT one of the exception types converted to JWTClaimsError at jwt.py:451 -- an unhandled exception propagating out of jwt.decode(), a remote DoS / error-handling defect for any caller that passes access_token. Fix: derive the digest from the signature algorithm that was actually verified (the alg matched against the caller's allow-list), and use .get() with an explicit rejection rather than a bare subscript.

leads.text: RSA signature algorithm confusion in the pure-Python fallback backend: jose/backends/rsa_backend.py:210 (RSAKey.verify, method line 206) calls 'pyrsa.verify(msg, sig, self._prepared_key)' and DISCARDS the return value. python-rsa's verify() returns the name of the hash algorithm it recovered from the PKCS#1 v1.5 DigestInfo structure, and it accepts ANY hash algorithm it supports -- it does not constrain the digest to the one the caller expects. Because this result is never compared against self.hash_alg (the digest implied by the JWS 'alg' header, e.g. RS256 vs RS384 vs RS512), a signature legitimately produced over the same signing input with a different/weaker digest is accepted as valid for the claimed algorithm. Combined with the fact that the JWS 'alg' is read from the attacker-controlled header (jose/jws.py:250 'header.get("alg")', centrality 0.000459) and that jws._verify_signature only restricts it when the caller actually passes a non-None algorithms allow-list ('algorithms is not None and alg not in algorithms', jws.py:254), an attacker can present a token whose header claims one RSA algorithm while the signature's embedded DigestInfo names another. Note this backend is only active when the 'cryptography' package is absent. Fix: compare pyrsa.verify's returned hash name against the expected self.hash_alg and reject on mismatch.

leads.text: Non-constant-time comparison of the at_hash claim: jose/jwt.py:453 compares the token's claim against the locally computed digest with 'claims["at_hash"] != expected_hash' instead of a constant-time comparison. expected_hash is derived from the access_token (a bearer credential) at jwt.py:448 via calculate_at_hash, so the byte-wise short-circuit leaks match-prefix length about a value derived from that credential, and it allows an attacker iteratively guessing at_hash values to confirm progress one byte at a time. Lower severity than the JWE tag issue because at_hash is a binding check rather than the primary authenticator, and the digest is of a token the presenter typically already holds -- reported for completeness since the same file/compare pattern as lead 3 and the codebase demonstrably has hmac.compare_digest available (native.py:69) and unused here. Fix: use hmac.compare_digest.

leads.text: Unbounded big-integer construction from JWK fields reachable on the verification path: jose/backends/rsa_backend.py:179-197 and jose/backends/cryptography_backend.py:278-302 feed JWK dictionary members straight into base64_to_long -- e.g. 'base64_to_long(jwk_dict.get("n"))' (rsa_backend.py:180, centrality 0.0000844), 'base64_to_long(jwk_dict.get("e"))' (rsa_backend.py:179), and p/q/dp/dq/qi at cryptography_backend.py:298-302. base64_to_long (jose/utils.py:33) applies no length cap: it does data.encode("ascii") (line 35), base64.urlsafe_b64decode (line 38), struct.unpack("%sB" % len(_d), _d) (line 39) and int_arr_to_long, which builds a hex string and calls int(..., 16) (utils.py:30) over the full attacker-sized buffer. A multi-megabyte 'n' therefore produces a huge Python int and quadratic-time parsing plus subsequent modular arithmetic, burning CPU and memory. IMPORTANT SCOPING CAVEAT that lowers my confidence: I queried jws._get_keys (jose/jws.py:217-246) and confirmed python-jose does NOT honor embedded 'jwk'/'jku' token headers -- key material comes only from the caller's 'key' argument -- so this is NOT attacker-controlled by the token alone. It becomes attacker-reachable only in host applications that pass a remotely fetched / user-supplied JWKS into jwt.decode/jws.verify. A verifier should confirm that precondition before treating this as exploitable. Fix: bound the accepted length of JWK numeric members before conversion.

leads.text: The guard that stops an asymmetric public key from being used as an HMAC shared secret has an INCOMPLETE blocklist: in BOTH HMAC backends `invalid_strings` is exactly [b"-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----", b"-----BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY-----", b"-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----", b"ssh-rsa"]. The OpenSSH public-key prefixes b"ecdsa-sha2-nistp256" / b"ecdsa-sha2-nistp384" / b"ecdsa-sha2-nistp521" and b"ssh-ed25519" are ABSENT, so an OpenSSH-format ECDSA/Ed25519 public key passes the check at native.py:46 / cryptography_backend.py:562 and is accepted as the HMAC secret. Combined with jwk.construct() selecting the key class purely from the algorithm name (jwk.py:76 `key_class = get_key(algorithm)`, jwk.py:79 `key_class(key_data, algorithm)`) and jws._sig_matches_keys calling `jwk.construct(key, alg)` at jws.py:208 with `alg` taken from the attacker-controlled JWS header (jws.py:250 `alg = header.get("alg")`), a verifier configured with a public OpenSSH ECDSA key and an algorithms list containing an HS* entry can be made to HMAC-verify with that public (attacker-known) key as the secret, letting the attacker forge arbitrary tokens.

leads.text: The JWS algorithm allowlist is conditionally skipped rather than mandatory. jws._verify_signature guards the allowlist check with `algorithms is not None and alg not in algorithms` at jws.py:254 — the `algorithms is not None` conjunct means that whenever the caller passes algorithms=None, NO allowlist is enforced at all and the attacker-controlled header `alg` (jws.py:250 `alg = header.get("alg")`) is honoured, selecting the key class via jwk.construct(key, alg) at jws.py:208. The code's own structure proves algorithms=None is a supported call shape. The only unconditional check is that `alg` be non-empty (jws.py:251-252), not that it be expected. jwt.decode forwards its algorithms argument through unchanged (jwt.py:141 `jws.verify(token, key, algorithms, verify=verify_signature)`), so a caller omitting the algorithms argument gets signature verification driven entirely by the attacker's header. A verifier should confirm the declared default of the `algorithms` parameter in the jws.verify / jwt.decode signatures (the graph elides it as `def decode(...)` at jwt.py:55).
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (m:CpgMethod {scan_id:$scan_id})-[:CONTAINS_CALL]->(c:CpgCall) WHERE m.file_path='jose/jws.py' AND m.name='_verify_signature' AND c.line >= 250 RETURN c.code, c.line ORDER BY line  -->  :250 `alg = header.get("alg")`, :251 `not alg`, :252 `raise JWSError("No algorithm was specified in the JWS header.")`, :254 `algorithms is not None and alg not in algorithms` AND the separate conjunct rows `algorithms is not None` / `alg not in algorithms`, :255 `raise JWSError("The specified alg value is not allowed")`, :257 `keys = _get_keys(key)`, :259 `not _sig_matches_keys(keys, signing_input, signature, alg)`. Query (jwt.py decode) --> :141 `payload = jws.verify(token, key, algorithms, verify = verify_signature)`. Parameter-default lookup attempted via MATCH (p:CpgParameter) and via CpgCall at jwt.py:55 --> only `decode = def decode(...)`, default not represented in graph.

leads.text: jwe.decrypt() provides no caller-supplied algorithm allowlist — unlike jws.verify, which takes an `algorithms` parameter. jwe.decrypt reads both `alg` and `enc` from the attacker-controlled JWE header (jwe.py:90 `alg = header["alg"]`, jwe.py:91 `enc = header["enc"]`) and validates them ONLY against the library-wide superset ALGORITHMS.SUPPORTED (jwe.py:92 and jwe.py:94). There is no mechanism for the application to restrict decryption to the single alg/enc pair it actually provisioned, so an attacker can freely steer the key-management path — e.g. between the ALGORITHMS.DIR branch (jwe.py:120), the key-unwrap branch (jwe.py:134 `key.unwrap_key(encrypted_key)`), and the AES-CBC-HMAC vs GCM content-encryption branches (jwe.py:230/233) — reaching the weaker CBC-HMAC code path and its non-constant-time tag compare and decrypt-then-verify ordering even when the deployment only intended GCM.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (m:CpgMethod {scan_id:$scan_id})-[:CONTAINS_CALL]->(c:CpgCall) WHERE m.file_path='jose/jwe.py' AND m.name='decrypt' RETURN c.code, c.line ORDER BY line  -->  :79 `tmp0 = _jwe_compact_deserialize(jwe_str)`, :90 `alg = header["alg"]`, :91 `enc = header["enc"]`, :92 `alg not in ALGORITHMS.SUPPORTED`, :93 raise JWEError, :94 `enc not in ALGORITHMS.SUPPORTED`, :95 raise JWEError, :101 `key = jwk.construct(key, alg)`, :120 `alg == ALGORITHMS.DIR`, :134 `cek_bytes = key.unwrap_key(encrypted_key)`. leads.text: Audience validation fails open on an absent `aud` claim. jwt._validate_aud (jwt.py:316) returns early at jwt.py:336 when `"aud" not in claims`, and the graph shows NO call of any kind between the function definition at line 316 and that check at 336 — i.e. there is no `if audience: raise JWTClaimsError(...)` guard. A token minted by the same issuer for a different relying party, or a general-purpose token with no aud, is accepted as if it were audience-scoped — cross-service token replay.

leads.text: No `crit` (critical header parameter) validation anywhere in the library, violating RFC 7515 s4.1.11 / RFC 7516 s4.1.13, which require an implementation to REJECT a JWS/JWE whose header contains a `crit` list naming extensions it does not understand. jws._load (jws.py:172-202) fully parses and JSON-decodes the header and validates only that it is a Mapping (jws.py:189-190), and jws._verify_signature inspects only `alg`; jwe.decrypt inspects only `alg`, `enc` and `zip`. A token can therefore assert `{"alg":"HS256","crit":["exp_policy"],...}` and python-jose will silently ignore the extension the producer marked as mandatory-to-understand, so a security-relevant header extension an upstream issuer relies on is dropped rather than causing rejection.

leads.text: The guard that blocks an asymmetric/public key from being used as an HMAC shared secret is implemented as a 4-entry substring DENYLIST that is incomplete: `invalid_strings = [b"-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----", b"-----BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY-----", b"-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----", b"ssh-rsa"]`. It omits every OpenSSH non-RSA public-key prefix -- `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256` / `ecdsa-sha2-nistp384` / `ecdsa-sha2-nistp521`, `ssh-ed25519`, `ssh-dss` -- and also `-----BEGIN EC PUBLIC KEY-----`. The error string ("The specified key is an asymmetric key or x509 certificate and should not be used as an HMAC secret.") proves the authors already knew asymmetric-key-as-HMAC-secret is an attack, yet only partially closed it. Because jose/jws.py:208 does `key = jwk.construct(key, alg)` with `alg` taken straight from the attacker-supplied JWS header (jose/jws.py:250 `alg = header.get("alg")`), an attacker who knows a server's OpenSSH-format ECDSA/Ed25519 PUBLIC key can submit a token with `alg: HS256`, have that public key coerced into an HMACKey, and forge a signature the server accepts -- classic algorithm confusion. The identical incomplete denylist is duplicated in both HMAC backends, so switching backends does not help. This is the CVE-2024-33663 class.

leads.text: In jose/jwe.py `_decrypt_and_auth` the authentication check runs AFTER decryption instead of before it: line 239 `plaintext = encryption_key.decrypt(cipher_text, iv, aad, auth_tag)` executes first, and only at line 240 is `auth_tag != auth_tag_check` evaluated. Any distinguishable behaviour from that premature decrypt (padding exception vs. tag exception, or differing timing/error paths) is a padding oracle permitting plaintext recovery and ciphertext forgery. Note the GCM branch sets `auth_tag_check = auth_tag` (line 235), making the line-240 comparison tautological for GCM, so line 240 is the ONLY integrity gate for the CBC-HMAC suites and it fires too late.

leads.text: jose/jws.py `_sig_matches_keys` wraps the signature-verification call in a bare catch-all that silently discards every exception: line 210 `key.verify(signing_input, signature)` inside a try whose handler is a lone `pass` at line 213. This is the highest-centrality reachable call in the entire scan (centrality 9.255e-5 at line 210, hop=1) -- i.e. essentially every attacker path funnels through it -- so a swallowed failure here has maximum blast radius. Because the handler catches everything rather than a narrow signature-mismatch error, genuine faults (a malformed/hostile key, a backend crypto error, a programming error in a key constructor, jose/jws.py:208 `jwk.construct(key, alg)` raising) are indistinguishable from a legitimate 'this key did not match' and are converted into a silent skip of that key. If attacker-influenced input can make verification raise rather than cleanly return False for every candidate key, the loop exits with no diagnostic and the only signal left is the aggregate `not _sig_matches_keys(...)` at line 259 -- destroying the audit trail and risking a fail-open if any caller or future refactor treats 'no key matched' as 'nothing was wrong'. leads.text: Incomplete denylist literal enables JWS algorithm confusion / signature forgery. HMACKey.__init__ guards against an asymmetric public key being misused as an HMAC secret using the literal list `invalid_strings = [b"-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----", b"-----BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY-----", b"-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----", b"ssh-rsa"]` (jose/backends/native.py:39, duplicated verbatim at jose/backends/cryptography_backend.py:555). The list omits every non-RSA OpenSSH public-key prefix: `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`, `ecdsa-sha2-nistp384`, `ecdsa-sha2-nistp521`, `ssh-ed25519`, `ssh-dss`, and `-----BEGIN PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK-----`. The membership test at native.py:46 is `any(string_value in key for string_value in invalid_strings)`, so an OpenSSH-format ECDSA public key passes validation and is accepted as the HMAC shared secret. An attacker who knows the victim's (public) ECDSA key can forge an `alg:HS256` token that verifies. This is the known python-jose <=3.3.0 algorithm-confusion issue (version confirmed as 3.3.0 at jose/__init__.py:1). The guard sits on a high-centrality chokepoint (HMACKey.__init__ centrality 2.83e-4), so the blast radius covers all verification paths.

leads.text: The `RSA1_5` algorithm literal is mapped to PKCS#1 v1.5 padding and left in the default SUPPORTED set, exposing a Bleichenbacher/Marvin padding-oracle primitive on an attacker-reachable decryption path. `jose/backends/cryptography_backend.py:223` defines `RSA1_5 = padding.PKCS1v15()`; line 238 builds `self.padding = {ALGORITHMS.RSA1_5: self.RSA1_5, ALGORITHMS.RSA_OAEP: ..., ALGORITHMS.RSA_OAEP_256: ...}.get(algorithm)`, keyed on the attacker-chosen JWE `alg` header. `CryptographyRSAKey.unwrap_key` (line 401) then performs `self.prepared_key.decrypt(wrapped_key, self.padding)` at line 403. Because `constants.py:54` puts `RSA1_5` in `RSA_KW` and `constants.py:70` unions `RSA_KW` into `ALGORITHMS.SUPPORTED`, an attacker can force the RSA1_5 branch and submit chosen ciphertexts; distinguishable padding-failure versus MAC-failure behaviour yields an oracle recovering the wrapped CEK.

leads.text: Unpinned / permissively-constrained cryptographic dependencies allow installation of known-vulnerable versions. The Dependency set declares `rsa` with an empty version constraint, `pycryptodome` with an empty constraint, `pyasn1` with an empty constraint, and `ecdsa` as `!= 0.15` — an exclusion of exactly one bad release rather than a minimum floor. An empty or exclusion-only constraint resolves to whatever the index offers and permits downgrade attacks or stale lockfiles pulling e.g. `rsa` <4.7 (CVE-2020-25658 Bleichenbacher timing, CVE-2020-13757), `pycryptodome` <3.19.1 (CVE-2023-52323 OAEP side channel), or `ecdsa` 0.13.x (CVE-2019-14853, CVE-2019-14859); note also that python-ecdsa has no fixed release for CVE-2024-23342 (Minerva timing). `ecdsa` and `rsa` are confirmed live imports, so these are runtime crypto dependencies, not test-only.

leads.text: SHA-1 hash literals are baked into the RSA-OAEP padding construction: `jose/backends/cryptography_backend.py:224` is `RSA_OAEP = padding.OAEP(padding.MGF1(hashes.SHA1()), hashes.SHA1(), None)`, using SHA-1 for both the MGF1 mask-generation function and the OAEP label hash. RFC 7518 does specify SHA-1 for the `RSA-OAEP` JWE algorithm, so this literal is spec-conformant and is reported only as a weak-primitive observation, not an exploitable flaw; the `RSA_OAEP_256` variant at line 225 correctly uses SHA-256. Flagging because a deprecated-hash literal in a crypto construction is the kind of pattern-in-data a reviewer should consciously accept rather than overlook.
